claims.text: Powder metallurgy, relative to conventional casting, induces a refined microstructure in a lightweight high-entropy alloy.
Powder metallurgy produces uniformly distributed nanoscale oxide precipitates in the alloy.
The refined microstructure and nanoscale oxide precipitates simultaneously improve strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance without compromising low density.
A conventionally cast alloy of the proposed composition has a coarse-grained, heterogeneous microstructure.
Fine grains and dispersed nanoscale oxide particles impede dislocation motion.
Dispersed nanoscale oxide particles provide sites for the formation of continuous protective surface films.
Microstructural refinement increases mechanical strength by impeding dislocation motion.
Nanoscale oxides form robust, adherent surface layers that enhance both corrosion and oxidation resistance.
A consistent distribution of reinforcing precipitates offsets property trade-offs normally associated with low-density materials.
The powder-metallurgy alloy will have greater yield strength than the compositionally identical cast alloy.
The powder-metallurgy alloy will have greater toughness than the compositionally identical cast alloy.
The powder-metallurgy alloy will exhibit improved corrosion resistance through reduced pit initiation.
The powder-metallurgy alloy will exhibit superior high-temperature oxidation resistance through stable protective surface oxides.
Powder-metallurgy processing will maintain the alloy's low overall density.
The conventionally cast baseline typically has a coarser and less uniform microstructure with fewer protective nanoscale oxides.
Scaling up powder metallurgy can cause excessive porosity that prevents the targeted microstructural refinement.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates can coarsen during prolonged high-temperature exposure.

If processing does not generate substantial refinement and stable nanoscale oxides, the processed alloy will not surpass the cast alloy in the combined properties of strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
Excessive oxide coarsening at temperatures above intended service temperatures degrades the protective effects.
The extent of grain refinement and the stability of nanoscale oxide precipitates vary with subtle changes in processing parameters.

contradictions.description: Maintaining low density is a predicted outcome, but the proposed experiment includes no density measurement, so that part of the prediction is not tested.

Improved toughness is predicted, but the listed mechanical measurements are yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation; no direct toughness or fracture-toughness measurement is specified.

Failure to generate the proposed microstructural mediator is treated as a boundary condition under which the hypothesis ceases to apply, but it is also included as a required part of the stated falsification result. This conflates failure to implement the intervention with falsification of the mediator-to-property mechanism.
